queue.title: A Recovery Drill Only Works If It Surprises You
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

A cyber drill that goes perfectly by script signals a too-lenient scenario, not real readiness. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

A cyber incident drill that goes perfectly according to script is more likely a sign of too lenient a scenario than real readiness.

A test of a cyber incident response plan that goes perfectly according to script, without a single moment of confusion or unexpected obstacle, more often points to too lenient a test than to real organisational readiness.

The value of a drill lies precisely in uncovering weak points before a real incident, so a scenario that deliberately includes unforeseen elements gives a more reliable picture of a system's actual resilience.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

A recovery drill that unfolds exactly as scripted tests the team's ability to perform a rehearsed routine, not its actual readiness for the unexpected — and unexpected is precisely what a real incident will be.

Building genuine unpredictability into a drill requires deliberate effort — someone has to design a scenario that even the exercise's organisers have not fully rehearsed — which is precisely why so many organisations default to the easier, scripted version instead. The extra effort pays off only when it matters least visibly: not in the drill itself, but in how the team performs during the real incident that the drill was meant to prepare them for.

queue.title: Least-Privilege Access Is Not Distrust
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Limiting data access to what is needed for the job is often wrongly read as distrust. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

Limiting data access strictly to what's needed for the job is often wrongly perceived as personal distrust toward employees.

The principle of least privilege, under which every employee and system receives only the data access genuinely required to do their job, is sometimes misread within organisational culture as an expression of distrust.

In practice, consistent application of this principle also protects employees themselves, since it reduces their exposure to accountability in the event of a security incident occurring outside their actual scope of work.

Limiting access to only what someone actually needs for their job is often mistaken as a sign of distrust toward the employee, when it is in fact standard practice that protects both the organisation and the employee from responsibility for systems outside their remit.

When someone holds access significantly broader than their tasks require, the circle of suspects and the number of possible causes unnecessarily grows in the event of a security incident — narrower access actually simplifies the investigation if a problem ever arises.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

When someone holds access significantly broader than their actual tasks require, the pool of possible causes in any security incident grows unnecessarily — narrower access simplifies the investigation if a problem ever arises.

Framing access limits this way — as a system-design principle rather than a judgement about any individual — helps organisations apply the principle consistently, including to senior staff who might otherwise be granted broad access simply as a matter of seniority rather than actual operational need.

queue.title: A Decision Made Quickly Is Not Necessarily a Bad One
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Decision speed and quality are often seen as opposites, but both depend on prior preparation. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

Decision speed and decision quality are often wrongly seen as opposites, though in practice both depend on preparation done before the moment of decision.

Organisations that have clearly predefined criteria and boundaries for particular types of decisions can decide quickly without sacrificing quality, since most of the analytical work was done before the specific situation arose.

Slowness in decision-making is often not a sign of thoroughness, but a consequence of lacking clear, pre-agreed frameworks within which a decision can be made quickly yet responsibly.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

An experienced team recognises the difference between 'fast because we already considered everything' and 'fast because we didn't have time to consider anything' — the first is a sign of maturity, the second a sign of risk that rarely reveals itself immediately.

An experienced team recognises the difference between 'fast because we already considered everything' and 'fast because we didn't have time to' — the first is maturity, the second is risk that rarely shows itself immediately.

Building the frameworks that make speed safe takes time upfront, which is precisely why organisations under constant pressure to show results often skip that step, and pay for it later.

Deliberation that happened when the framework was built lets what looks like a fast decision in the moment actually be the fast execution of a decision already made earlier, under calmer conditions.

Sooner or later, an organisation that consistently skips this preparation pays for it, one slow, high-stakes decision at a time, exactly when speed would have mattered most.

The gap between the two situations is rarely visible in the moment itself; it only becomes clear afterward, when the same decision either holds up or has to be revisited.

queue.title: An AI That Explains Its Decision Beats a More Accurate One
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

The ability to explain a model's recommendation is often worth more than marginal accuracy gains. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

In a business context, the ability to explain why a model made a given recommendation is often more valuable than marginally better statistical accuracy.

When choosing between two models of similar performance, the one that can explain its recommendation in understandable language usually delivers greater real value than one that is marginally more accurate but completely opaque.

The ability to explain allows the accountable person to review the logic before making the final decision, rather than accepting the model's recommendation without any real means of verification.

A model that cannot explain why it recommended something forces an organisation into blind trust — and blind trust in a system that occasionally errs means the mistake surfaces only after it has already caused damage.

An explainable model also enables regulatory compliance: when an auditor or regulator asks for justification, the organisation needs more than 'the system calculated it that way'.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

An explainable model also supports regulatory compliance: when an auditor asks for justification, an organisation needs more than 'the system calculated it that way' — it needs a traceable reason.

This preference for explainability over marginal accuracy is not a rejection of performance — it is a recognition that a system's practical value depends on whether people actually trust and use its output, and trust is built through understanding, not through a performance benchmark that most users never see and could not evaluate even if they did.

A model that cannot explain why it recommended something forces an organisation into blind trust — and blind trust in a system that occasionally errs means the mistake surfaces only after it has already caused damage.

An explainable model also supports regulatory compliance: when an auditor asks for justification, an organisation needs more than 'the system calculated it that way'.

queue.title: Energy Efficiency Is Not Just a Cost, It's Also a Risk
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Energy efficiency viewed only as a cost, not as resilience against price shocks, misses part of the picture. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

Organisations viewing energy efficiency purely through the lens of cost, not resilience to future price shocks, are underestimating part of the real picture.

Investment in energy efficiency is often, in internal discussion, reduced solely to the question of cost and payback period, while the dimension of reduced exposure to future, hard-to-predict energy price shocks is overlooked.

An organisation less dependent on energy price volatility also has greater operational stability during periods of external disruption beyond its control.

An organisation that views energy efficiency purely as a cost-saving measure overlooks that dependence on cheap but unstable energy is itself a source of operational risk once conditions in the energy market shift.

Investment in efficiency and diversified energy sources should therefore be measured as a reduction in risk exposure, not only as a reduction in the bill — the two effects rarely align on the same timeline, but both are real.

An organisation that treats energy efficiency purely as a cost-saving measure overlooks that dependence on cheap but unstable energy is itself a source of operational risk once energy market conditions shift.

Investment in efficiency and diversified energy sources should therefore be measured both as risk reduction and cost reduction — the two effects rarely align on the same timeline, but both are real.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

This reframing changes how efficiency investments get evaluated internally: rather than competing against other cost-saving initiatives purely on payback period, they should also be weighed against the cost of remaining exposed to energy market volatility that efficiency investment would have reduced.

queue.title: Ownership Visible in the Registry Builds Trust
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

When ownership can be verified in a public registry, statements about transparency become redundant. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

When real ownership and governance structure can be verified in a public registry, statements about transparency become redundant.

When a partner or investor can independently verify the real ownership and governance structure in a publicly available registry, additional statements about the organisation's transparency become almost superfluous.

Organisations that actively point to public registries as a source of verification, rather than asking to be taken at their word, in practice build a stronger foundation for a long-term business relationship.

A partner who can independently verify an ownership structure through a public registry, without needing to trust statements in a presentation, enters the relationship with less uncertainty — and less uncertainty usually means a faster decision to cooperate.

An organisation that keeps its ownership structure clean and easily verifiable sends a clear signal that it has nothing to hide — a signal worth more than any transparency statement written into its own marketing material.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

An organisation that keeps its ownership structure clean and easily verifiable in public registers sends a clear signal that it has nothing to hide — a signal worth more than any statement of transparency in its own marketing material.

Maintaining this clarity requires ongoing attention — corporate structures naturally become more complex over time as subsidiaries are added or roles change — which is why treating registry accuracy as a one-time filing rather than an ongoing discipline is a common and avoidable failure.

An investor who cannot independently confirm an ownership structure through a public registry, and must instead rely on statements in a presentation, enters the relationship carrying more uncertainty than necessary.

Maintaining that clarity requires ongoing attention, since corporate structures naturally grow more complex over time as subsidiaries are added or roles change within a group.

queue.title: System Integration Matters as Much as the Systems
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Poorly connected tools often make an organisation less effective than a simpler, integrated system. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

An organisation with several excellent but poorly connected digital tools is often less effective than one with a simpler, well-integrated system.

An organisation using several individually excellent but poorly connected digital tools is, in practice, often less operationally effective than one using a simpler but well-integrated system.

Integration quality, meaning the ease with which data flows between different parts of the business system, directly affects how much time is spent on manual reconciliation instead of real analytical work.

The best individual system loses much of its value if data must be manually transferred to another system, because every manual transfer introduces delay and a chance for error that an automated integration simply does not have.

Evaluating new technology cannot stop at 'is this system good on its own' — it must also ask 'what will it cost to make it talk to everything else we already use', since integration cost often exceeds the cost of the licence itself.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

Evaluating new technology cannot stop at 'is this system good on its own' — it must also ask 'what will it cost to make this talk to everything else we already use', since integration cost often exceeds the licence itself.

Factoring integration cost into technology evaluation from the outset, rather than discovering it after a purchase has already been made, prevents the common pattern of a technically excellent system delivering disappointing real-world value because it was never properly connected to what it needed to work alongside.

queue.title: The Line Between Suggestion and Decision Must Stay Visible
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Losing the line between an AI suggestion and a human decision makes accountability hard to establish. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

When internal communication loses the distinction between what a model proposed and what a person decided, accountability becomes hard to establish.

In organisations that intensively use AI tools to prepare analyses and recommendations, there is a risk that, over time, the clear line between what the system proposed and what the accountable employee actually decided gets lost.

Consistently labelling every AI-generated suggestion as such, until it is formally confirmed by the accountable person, maintains a clear line of accountability even when the model was used at an early stage of decision preparation.

When a system automatically turns a suggestion into a recorded decision without a clear step of human confirmation, that boundary gradually fades from the user's awareness, until they stop meaningfully questioning what has been proposed to them.

A visible boundary means the interface clearly distinguishes 'this is a recommendation' from 'this is the decision you made' — a difference that looks cosmetic but directly determines whether anyone actually re-examines a result or simply confirms it by reflex.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

A visible boundary means the user interface clearly distinguishes 'this is a recommendation' from 'this is the decision you made' — a distinction that looks cosmetic but directly affects whether anyone actually re-examines the output or simply confirms it by reflex.

Maintaining this visible boundary requires deliberate interface design, not just good intentions — a system that technically allows a human override but makes exercising it inconvenient will, in practice, see that override used less and less often over time.

queue.title: A Board That Asks No Questions Is a Risk, Not Support
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Decisions that go unquestioned are often mistaken for unity, but reflect a lack of real oversight. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

A culture where one person's decisions are rarely questioned is often mistaken for unity, when in practice it reflects an absence of real oversight.

When management or director decisions are not systematically questioned, this is sometimes interpreted as a sign of unity and trust, when in fact it represents the absence of a mechanism that would catch a more serious error in time.

A healthy organisational culture encourages constructive questioning of business decisions, regardless of the hierarchical position of the person making them, because this very practice reduces the likelihood of costly mistakes.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

The value of a board is not measured by how quickly it approves proposals, but by the quality of the questions it asks before approval — an organisation whose board asks hard questions early is less often blindsided by hard surprises later.

A board that treats every management proposal as a formality to be rubber-stamped is not providing oversight; it is removing the one independent check the organisation has, without anyone formally deciding to remove it. That absence becomes visible only after a decision no one challenged has already caused damage, at which point the question is no longer whether the board should have asked more, but why it didn't. Building a board culture where difficult questions are expected, not resented, is one of the cheapest forms of risk management available to any organisation, and one of the most consistently neglected.

A board that rubber-stamps every management proposal is not providing support; it removes the one independent check the organisation has, without anyone formally deciding to remove it.

Building a board culture where difficult questions are expected, not resented, is one of the cheapest forms of risk management available to any organisation, and one of the most consistently neglected.

queue.title: A Sustainability Report Should Admit Its Shortcomings
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

A sustainability report with only positive results loses credibility with careful readers. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

A report listing only positive results, without a single area for improvement, loses credibility with a careful reader.

A sustainability report that lists only positive results, without a single mention of an area requiring further improvement, usually raises doubt about the completeness of the picture in a careful reader, rather than trust.

Acknowledging concrete shortcomings, alongside a clear plan to address them, typically comes across as more credible than a report that appears as if the organisation has already achieved perfection in every measured area.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

Acknowledging a shortfall, paired with a concrete plan for addressing it, builds more credibility than any run of favourable figures alone — because the reader then knows the report is a genuine account, not a marketing document.

Readers, investors, and regulators increasingly recognise the pattern of a report that lists only achievements, and that recognition itself has become a credibility risk — a suspiciously flawless report now invites more scrutiny, not less. An organisation that gets ahead of this by candidly naming where it still falls short, alongside a specific plan and timeline for improvement, converts a potential weakness into a demonstration of exactly the kind of governance maturity that sustainability reporting is meant to signal in the first place.
